record.paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
record.context_brief: Residual population structure in GWAS and PRS
record.original_question: How can association and prediction studies of complex human traits fully control residual population structure—the confounding that arises because ancestry or family identity affects both genotype and environmental exposure—without overcorrecting away real genetic signal, so that very large genome-wide association studies and polygenic risk scores do not produce spurious associations or biased predictions?

evidence.quote: the precise family and ethnic identity of an individual (generally simply referred to as their “population” or “ancestry”) is a suspect confounder for any genetic association, as it affects the environment which an individual is born into (e.g., weather, nutrition, etc.) and, as a result, can affect the studied trait

there are increasing concerns that residual population structure can still lead to spurious associations, especially with very large cohorts that are now emerging (open problem #1: population structure; Fig. 1B).

It is still not fully understood how residual population structure affects the results of GWAS and polygenic risk scores. More research is also needed for establishing new methods and practices to address the problem.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a population of N individuals indexed by i = 1,...,N. For each individual, let g_i ∈ {0,1,2}^M denote a vector of genotypes at M biallelic loci, let y_i ∈ ℝ denote a quantitative trait value, and let a_i denote a (latent) ancestry/family-identity variable taking values in some space A. Assume a generative model

  y_i = Σ_{j=1}^M β_j g_{ij} + e(a_i) + ε_i,

where β = (β_1,…,β_M) is the vector of true causal genetic effects, e: A → ℝ is an unknown environmental effect that depends on ancestry/family identity (because ancestry influences environmental exposures such as climate, nutrition, social context), and ε_i is independent noise. The genotypes also depend on a_i, so that g_i and e(a_i) are statistically dependent through the shared latent ancestry, creating confounding.

A genome-wide association study (GWAS) estimates marginal or joint regressions of y on g; a polygenic risk score (PRS) for a new individual with genotype g* is a linear predictor Σ_j β̂_j g*_j formed from such estimates.

Standard correction methods (e.g., including top principal components of the genotype matrix, linear mixed models with a genetic relatedness matrix, family-based tests, LD-score regression intercepts) reduce but do not eliminate the dependence between estimated effects and a_i; this remaining confounding is called residual population structure. Overcorrection — for example, projecting out too many directions correlated with a_i — can also remove a portion of the true signal Σ_j β_j g_{ij} when β has components aligned with population-differentiated allele-frequency directions.

Problem. Develop a statistical framework and an associated estimator β̂ (and corresponding PRS predictor) such that, under explicit and realistic assumptions on the joint distribution of (g_i, a_i, e(a_i), ε_i) — including very large sample sizes N where biases dominate sampling variance —:

(a) β̂ is a consistent (or provably low-bias) estimator of the causal effects β, controlling all spurious associations induced by residual population structure;

(b) the procedure does not systematically attenuate components of β that are correlated with population-frequency differentiation (i.e., it avoids overcorrection of true genetic signal);

(c) the resulting PRS achieves prediction accuracy in target populations that is unbiased with respect to ancestry, with quantifiable guarantees on transferability across populations a ∈ A.

State precise sufficient conditions on the data-generating process, and either construct such a procedure with rigorous guarantees, or prove an impossibility/identifiability result delineating when consistent unconfounded estimation of β and ancestry-fair PRS prediction is achievable from observational genotype–phenotype data.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent literature (2022–2025) continues to document that residual population stratification biases GWAS effect estimates and PRS predictions, particularly in large biobanks, and that current corrections (PCA, LMMs, sib-based designs) only partially address the problem while sometimes overcorrecting. No consensus method or proof of identifiability has been established, so the problem is still considered open.

status_evidence.title: Stratification and PRS bias
status_evidence.snippet: Residual population stratification continues to bias polygenic predictions; current adjustments are incomplete.
status_evidence.claim: Residual structure remains a documented source of bias in PRS as of 2023–2024.

status_evidence.title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics (arXiv:2108.06684)
status_evidence.snippet: Open problem #1 lists residual population structure as not fully understood and in need of new methods.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is explicitly identified as open.

status_evidence.title: Sib-regression and overcorrection
status_evidence.snippet: Within-family analyses reduce stratification but at substantial cost to power and may attenuate signal.
status_evidence.claim: Existing corrections trade off bias and signal, supporting that the problem is unresolved.
